finding.claim: Unauthenticated /fetch endpoint passes the raw `target` query parameter to http.Get and returns the full response body to the caller, allowing full-read SSRF to loopback, RFC-1918, and cloud metadata endpoints. Redirects are followed with no re-validation.
finding.source: main.go:15 — r.URL.Query().Get("target"), reachable via route registered at main.go:41
finding.sink: main.go:16 — http.Get(target); response copied back at main.go:22 via io.Copy(w, resp.Body)

trace.note: http.HandleFunc("/fetch", fetch) exposes the handler with no authentication
target read from query string with no transformation
http.Get invoked with the raw attacker-supplied string; no scheme, host, or IP check
err.Error() returned to caller, enabling an internal port-scan oracle
full response body streamed back to the attacker (non-blind)

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, scheme check, host check, or authentication between source and sink. Go net/http only dispatches http/https, so file:// and other schemes fail. Redirects are followed by default with no CheckRedirect, so redirect-based pivoting to internal hosts is possible.

verdict.guard_found: none. The `allowed` hostname map (main.go:9-12) is only consulted in safeFetch (main.go:27), not in the vulnerable fetch handler. fetch (main.go:14-23) has no auth, scheme, host, or IP check, and http.Get uses default redirect-following with no CheckRedirect.
verdict.reason: The /fetch route (main.go:41) hands the unvalidated `target` query parameter (main.go:15) directly to http.Get (main.go:16), and the response body is streamed back to the caller (main.go:22), so the finding holds; the allowlist at main.go:9-12 guards only the separate /safe handler.
